unit.unitOverview: Four passive forms you have not met, and what each one claims. Say that something is being dealt with now, that it will be done next month, that it must be done by everybody, and that it had already been done before anybody noticed. Then judge a passive by whether a reader can check it.
unit.learningPath:
The lesson: listen first, then read it back.
Words: five groups, 29 words. Listen and say each one.
Patterns: 5 cards. Read the one done for you before you try.
Reading: a holding letter, a writing guide and an inspection report.
Questions: 10 about the three texts.
Speaking: tap the mic, say it, listen back.
Writing: four tasks, each with a model.
Practice and the check: 7 exercises, then 12 questions.

visual.lectureScript:
You have met the passive four times already, so let us be clear about what this unit adds.
Level 2 built the present and past passive. Unit 1 of this level put a person at the front. Unit 4 gave you the passive of rules and the one that names nobody at all.
What none of those could reach is four more forms, and all four are here.

The first is the one that is happening right now.
You can say every batch is inspected, which is a rule. You can say the batch was inspected, which is finished.
Neither of those can tell somebody that the work is going on at this moment, and official English needs that constantly.
The incident is being investigated. Three pieces instead of two: is, being, and the -ed form.
That being is the whole card, and it is what learners drop.
Listen to what happens without it. The incident is investigated. That now says every incident is investigated, routinely, which may well be true and is not what you meant.

The second is the future, and it is simpler than it looks.
Take any future you already have and put be plus the -ed form inside it.
Will becomes will be installed. Going to becomes is going to be shut down. The arranged continuous becomes is being resurfaced next week.
There is one thing worth noticing about why notices are written this way.
We will notify you puts the office first. You will be notified puts the reader first.
The reader is the one who needs to know, so the passive is the right choice, not a way of hiding.
And the rule from Unit 5 still holds. Once the parts have been delivered, work will restart. Never once the parts will have been delivered.

The third is the passive after a modal, and it never varies.
Modal, then be, then the -ed form.
Must be signed. Can be repaired. Should be reported. May be refused. Need not be returned.
Almost every rule in every official document you will ever read is built that way.
Two things to watch. The be is what disappears when you are writing quickly: the form must signed is the error.
And the not goes on the modal, not on the be. It must not be removed.
That pair from Unit 7 is still opposite in the passive. Must not be returned forbids it. Need not be returned makes it optional.

The fourth needs Unit 9, which is why this unit comes after it.
Has been, and had been.
The batch has been withdrawn reaches up to now. The guard had been removed marks the earlier of two past events.
And the error here is the same one as with being. Drop the been and the sentence changes voice.
The batch has withdrawn from sale says the batch withdrew itself, which is nonsense, and it is written every day.
Line all of them up, because a real report uses the whole set in one paragraph.
Is inspected, a rule. Is being inspected, now. Was inspected, finished with a time. Has been inspected, finished and still relevant. Had been inspected, finished before something else. Will be inspected, still to come.
One verb. Six sentences. Six different facts about the world.

The last card is the irregular comparative adverbs, and it finishes Unit 3.
Well becomes better and best. Badly becomes worse and worst. Far becomes further. Little becomes less. Much becomes more.
No rule predicts any of them, and they are among the most common words in the language, so they matter more than the regular ones do.
Watch the good and well pair. Good describes the person. Well describes the working.
She is a good worker and she works well. The comparative of the adverb is better, so she works better than he does.

One last thing, and it is the reading.
There is a kind of letter that is four sentences long, entirely passive, and tells you nothing.
The matter is being investigated. The findings will be reviewed in due course. You will be notified once a decision has been reached.
It would be easy to blame the passive for that, and it would be wrong.
Every one of those forms has a proper use, and the letter is grammatically excellent.
What makes it useless is that nothing in it can be checked. No name, no date, no number.
Add those three things and the same four sentences become a real answer.
Start with the words. Say each one aloud before you move on.

readings.title: The Reply That Says Nothing
readings.setting: An office, reading a holding letter
readings.passageScript:
I have kept one letter for years because it is a perfect example of its kind.
It is four sentences long and it tells you nothing at all, and every sentence in it is a passive.
The matter is being investigated. The findings will be reviewed in due course.
You will be notified once a decision has been reached. No further action can be taken at this stage.
Read those again and ask the question this course keeps asking. By whom?
Investigated by whom, reviewed by whom, notified by whom, and who decides what in due course means.
The letter names nobody, commits to no date, and accepts no responsibility.
It is not dishonest. Every sentence in it is probably true.
What I want to say about it is the thing people usually get wrong.
The passive is not the villain here. Every one of those four forms has a proper use.
The matter is being investigated is exactly right if a team is genuinely working on it and you cannot name them.
You will be notified is better than we will notify you, because the reader cares what happens to them.
What makes the letter useless is not the grammar. It is that nothing in it can be checked.
A good version would use the same four forms and add a name, a date and a number.

readings.title: Five Passives and What Each One Says
readings.setting: A page from a writing guide
readings.passageScript:
The passive is one pattern with several tenses, and each tense makes a different claim.
Every batch is inspected before dispatch. That is a rule. It holds on anybody's shift.
That batch is being inspected at the moment. That is now, and it is not finished.
The batch was inspected on Tuesday. That is a finished event with a time attached to it.
The batch has been inspected. That is finished, and it still matters, and no time is given.
The batch had been inspected before the fault was found. That is finished before something else.
Five sentences, one verb, and five different facts about the world.
Two of them are worth extra attention because learners collapse them.
Is inspected and is being inspected look almost identical and are far apart.
The first describes a routine that applies always. The second describes this one, right now.
Writing is inspected about a particular batch tells the reader it happens to every batch, which may be true and is not what you meant.
The other pair is has been and had been.
Dropping been from either turns the sentence active, and it then claims the batch acted on its own.

readings.passageScript:
INSPECTION REPORT — SITE 4
Period: April to June        Inspector: L. Nkemdirim        Issued: 8 July

1. Scope
All storage areas were examined. Records for the period were audited.
Two areas could not be inspected, as they were being resurfaced during the visit.

2. Findings
Two breaches of the storage procedure were identified.
Samples had been stored above four degrees for at least eleven days before the fault was noticed.
The temperature log had not been checked since 2 May.

3. Action taken
The affected batch has been withdrawn from sale and traced to a single supplier.
The monitoring unit is being replaced this week.

4. Required action
The log must be checked daily and signed. It must not be completed retrospectively.
A revised procedure is to be issued by 1 August.
The two outstanding areas will be inspected before the next quarter.

5. Sanction
No sanction has been applied. Compliance will be reviewed in October.
The site was managed better this quarter than last, and the remedy was agreed quickly.

grammar.title: It is being investigated: the passive while it is still happening
grammar.explanation:
You can build the passive in the present and the past: it is inspected,
it was inspected. Both describe a rule or a finished event.
Neither can say that the thing is going on RIGHT NOW, and a great deal of
official language needs exactly that.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
is or are + BEING + the past participle

The incident is being investigated.
The forms are being distributed this week.
The road is being resurfaced, so the entrance is closed.

And in the past, was or were + BEING:
The line was being inspected when the alarm sounded.
The records were being transferred at the time.

Compare the three, because each says something different:
The incident WAS investigated.       finished
The incident IS BEING investigated.  going on now
The incident HAS BEEN investigated.  finished, and it still matters

Where you meet it: notices, holding replies, news.
It is the standard way of saying we have started and we have not finished,
which is why it appears in almost every reply that answers nothing.
grammar.workedExample:
One done, step by step.
Make this passive, and say it is going on now: They are investigating the incident.
1. The thing goes to the front: the incident.
2. One thing, and it is now, so is.
3. Going on now needs being.
4. investigate becomes investigated.
Answer: The incident is being investigated.
They is dropped, because in a notice nobody needs to be told which department.

The being is what learners leave out, and without it the meaning changes.
No: The incident is investigated. (that says it happens routinely)
Yes: The incident is being investigated. (it is happening now)

grammar.title: It will be installed: the passive in the future
grammar.explanation:
Every future form you know has a passive, and they are built the same way:
take the future, and put BE plus the past participle after it.
Nothing below this unit teaches any of them, and a plan or a notice about
work to come is written in almost nothing else.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
will + BE + past participle
The new unit will be installed next month.
You will be notified in writing.
Nothing will be dispatched before Friday.

going to + BE + past participle
The line is going to be shut down for two days.

The present continuous passive, for an arrangement:
The road is being resurfaced next week. (already arranged)

And after a time word, where you already know not to use will:
Once the parts have been delivered, work will restart.
NOT: once the parts will have been delivered.

Why notices use it: the reader needs to know what will happen to THEM.
We will notify you puts the office first.
You will be notified puts the reader first, which is usually the point.
grammar.workedExample:
One done, step by step.
Write this as a notice: We are going to install the new unit next month.
1. The reader cares about the unit, not about us, so put the unit first.
2. Future with will: will be.
3. install becomes installed.
4. Drop we, because the notice does not need to say which team.
Answer: The new unit will be installed next month.
grammar.commonMistake:
Learners put will inside a time clause, exactly as with the active.
No: Once the parts will have been delivered, work will restart.
Yes: Once the parts have been delivered, work will restart.
The rule from Unit 5 applies to the passive unchanged.
grammar.memoryTip: Take any future form and slot BE plus the -ed form into it.

grammar.reviewStatus: Reviewed: script review and curriculum sign-off, 2026-08-01
grammar.title: It must be signed: the passive after a modal
grammar.explanation:
Every modal takes the same passive shape, and it never changes.
modal + BE + past participle.
This is how almost every rule, instruction and condition in an official
document is written, so it is worth being fast at.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
must be signed      can be repaired      should be reported
may be refused      might be delayed     cannot be traced
has to be inspected  need not be returned

The modal never changes, whoever or whatever the subject is:
It must be signed. They must be signed. She must be notified.

The negative goes on the MODAL, not on the be:
It must NOT be removed.   NOT: it must be not removed.
It cannot be traced.

Why a rule uses it: the rule binds the thing, not a named person.
You must sign the form.        (only true of you)
The form must be signed.       (true whoever presents it)

And the pair from Unit 7, in the passive, still means opposite things:
It must not be returned.  = returning it is forbidden
It need not be returned.  = returning it is optional
grammar.workedExample:
One done, step by step.

1. A rule should bind the form, not a particular person.
2. The thing goes first: every form.
3. The modal stays exactly as it is: must.
4. Add be, then the participle: be signed.
Answer: Every form must be signed before dispatch.
Somebody has gone, and the rule now holds whoever is on duty.
grammar.commonMistake:
The be is what disappears when learners are working quickly.
No: The form must signed before dispatch.
Yes: The form must be signed before dispatch.
A modal is always followed by a plain verb, and here the plain verb is be.
grammar.memoryTip: modal + be + the -ed form. The not goes on the modal.

1. Every form must be signed before dispatch.
2. Most of these can be repaired on site.

grammar.title: It has been withdrawn: the passive with a perfect
grammar.explanation:
Unit 9 gave you the past perfect. That form has a passive too, and so does
the present perfect you have had since Level 2.
These are the forms a report uses to say what has been done so far, and
what had already been done before something else happened.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
PRESENT PERFECT PASSIVE — has or have + BEEN + past participle
The batch has been withdrawn from sale.
Two breaches have been identified.
Nothing has been decided yet.
It reaches up to now, exactly as the active perfect does.

PAST PERFECT PASSIVE — had + BEEN + past participle
The guard had been removed before the shift began.
The records had already been transferred when the fault was found.
It marks the earlier of two past events, as in Unit 9.

Line them up, because a report uses all of them in one paragraph:
is inspected        a rule
is being inspected  now
was inspected       finished, at a stated time
has been inspected  finished, and still relevant
had been inspected  finished before something else
will be inspected   still to come
grammar.workedExample:
One done, step by step.
The guard came off before the shift. The shift began at two. Write it.
1. Two past events, and the removal came first.
2. Earlier takes the past perfect: had.
3. Passive needs been plus the participle: been removed.
4. The remover is unknown, so no by phrase.
Answer: The guard had been removed before the shift began.
That sentence is the reason a written statement is worth taking: it fixes the order.
grammar.commonMistake:
been is dropped, and the sentence becomes a different tense.
No: The batch has withdrawn from sale. (that says the batch withdrew itself)
Yes: The batch has been withdrawn from sale.
Without been it is an active perfect, and it means something else entirely.
grammar.memoryTip: has been for up to now. had been for before that. Never drop the been.

5. Nothing ___ (decide) yet.

7. The batch has withdrawn from sale.
8. The guard had removed before the shift.
grammar.answerKey:
1. has been withdrawn  2. had been removed  3. have been identified
4. had already been transferred  5. has been decided  6. is inspected
7. The batch has BEEN withdrawn.  8. The guard had BEEN removed.
In 7 and 8 the missing been turns a passive into an active, and the sentence
then claims the batch and the guard acted on their own.

grammar.title: Better, worse, further: the comparatives that do not follow the rule
grammar.explanation:
Unit 3 gave you not as quickly as, and less carefully.
Both of those are regular. A small group of adverbs have their own forms
that no rule predicts, and they are among the commonest words in English,
so the irregulars matter more than the regulars do.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
well   -> better   -> best
badly  -> worse    -> worst
far    -> further  -> furthest   (also farther, for distance)
little -> less     -> least
much   -> more     -> most

She did it better than I did. He took it worse than expected.
That is the batch that was inspected most thoroughly.

THE SUPERLATIVE takes the, and for long adverbs it takes the most:
the most carefully, the most thoroughly, the least often

Watch the pair learners swap:
good is an ADJECTIVE. well is the ADVERB.
She is a good worker. She works well.
So the comparative of the adverb is better: she works better than he does.

And the double frame, which is worth having:
The more carefully it is checked, the fewer faults are found.
The sooner it is reported, the better.
grammar.workedExample:
One done, step by step.

1. Are you describing the person or the working? The working.
2. The working takes an adverb, so well, not good.
3. The comparative of well is better.
Answer: She works better than he does.
She is better than he is would be about the people, which is a different claim.
grammar.commonMistake:
gooder and more well do not exist, and badder does not either.
No: She works more well than he does.
Yes: She works better than he does.
The irregular form replaces the whole pattern: no more, no -er.
grammar.memoryTip: Five irregulars carry most of the traffic. Learn them as a block.

grammar.answerKey:
1. better, best  2. worse, worst  3. further, furthest  4. less, least  5. more, most
6. better  7. worse  8. the most thoroughly (a superlative takes the)
9. better  10. good worker, works well
Number 10 is the pair: good describes the person, well describes the working.
8 or more right: good.
